extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of journalism and American history
extracted.subtask_description: A textbook account of the development of the partisan press in the early United States (late 18th century), covering editors, party newspapers, governmental responses, and the Alien and Sedition laws. Emphasizes norms, conflicts of interest, legal restrictions, and practical newsroom practices of the period.

rubrics_metrics.name: Press as a check on monarchy / duty to energize democracy
rubrics_metrics.description: The free press can 'save our Constitution' and 'energize the spirit of democracy' by checking tendencies toward monarchy and monocratic rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jefferson's view (reported here) holds that the press serves as a powerful corrective to concentration of power; newspapers' essays on equality and fraternity and praise of radical thinkers were seen as 'to energize the spirit of democracy.' The text uses Freneau and the National Gazette as examples of a paper that 'has been that paper which has checked the career of the monocrats.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Conflict of interest / government-paid editors
rubrics_metrics.description: Questioning the propriety of an editor who 'receives a salary from the government' publishing attacks on the administration — i.e., whether government payment creates an obligation or a disqualifying conflict.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hamilton's attack (signed 'T. L.') framed the issue as: 'Whether this salary is paid for translations or for publications the design of which is to vilify those to whom the voice of the people has committed the administration of our public affairs.' The passage shows this was a central normative and rhetorical point in disputes over partisan journalism and government patronage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sedition Act (July 14, 1798) — definition and penalties
rubrics_metrics.description: Made it a high misdemeanor, punishable by a fine of $5,000 and five years' imprisonment, to 'write, print, publish or quote any false scandal or scurrilous writings' against the government, the President, or either House of Congress, or to unlawfully conspire against the government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The law was aimed at suppressing opposition press (explicitly described as targeting the 'Whig press' and named individuals such as Bache). An amendment allowed the truth of the matter to be given in evidence as a defense, altering common-law libel practice. The text frames the acts as 'oppressive' and notes their severity and political motivation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alien Act — presidential power to expel aliens
rubrics_metrics.description: Authorized the President to order out of the country any aliens deemed 'dangerous to the peace and safety of the United States,' with refusal to depart punishable by up to three years' imprisonment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Described as 'without parallel in American legislation' and presented in the chapter as part of Federalist efforts to 'shackle the press' and suppress foreign (especially French) influence; used in the political context against perceived alien influence in republican papers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Amendment to libel law permitting truth as defense
rubrics_metrics.description: An amendment to the Sedition Act permitted the truth of the published matter to be offered in evidence as a good defense, thereby modifying the common law of libel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text notes Bayard's role in obtaining the amendment and situates it as a concession within otherwise severe sedition penalties; this is presented as a legal standard affecting how journalists could defend against prosecution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial partisanship and vituperative style — professional risks
rubrics_metrics.description: Extreme personal abuse, vituperation, and partisan attacks in newspapers carried real risks: libel suits, financial ruin, physical assaults, office wrecking, and suspension of publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Cobbett's Porcupine's Gazette suspended after a $5,000 libel verdict to Dr. Benjamin Rush; Bache was beaten and his office nearly wrecked after savage attacks; Aurora's office was 'very nearly demolish[ed]' after attacks on Washington. The text implies a normative caution that excessive personal invective has legal and social consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Newspapers as party organs / necessity of active combatants
rubrics_metrics.description: Party leaders believed it necessary to have active newspaper 'combatants' to reply to opposing journals and to energetically defend party positions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jefferson, Madison, and Lee concluded they 'must have an active combatant in the newspaper field' to answer Fenno and Hamilton; the establishment and financing of party papers (e.g., Webster's Minerva, Freneau's National Gazette) are given as tactical measures to shape public opinion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economical reuse of copy — subsidiary papers
rubrics_metrics.description: Technical/editorial practice of producing a subsidiary paper composed entirely from the columns of a primary paper without recomposition as a cost-saving device.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Noah Webster's introduction of the 'Herald' as a semi-weekly made up entirely from the Minerva's columns is presented as an 'economical device' — an example of pragmatic production practices in the periodical press.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presidential and governmental responsibility in press disputes
rubrics_metrics.description: The President and executive officials bear responsibility in managing press-related disputes among cabinet members and in responding to press attacks (e.g., Washington attempted to end bickering and later called for a neutral course regarding Genet).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The chapter frames episodes (Washington asking Hamilton and Jefferson to 'cease' bickering; Washington's proclamation of neutrality; his reaction to Freneau's attacks) as illustrating the executive's role and dilemmas when press and politics collide.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial accuracy and careful proofreading in official publications
rubrics_metrics.description: Careful proofreading and attention to punctuation and phrasing are important in official communications (e.g., Washington personally made 'but a few alterations' and was 'very minute' in punctuation of the Farewell Address).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claypoole's account of preparing Washington's Farewell Address emphasizes multiple proof stages and the President's detailed attention to punctuation, illustrating the standard of meticulous editorial practice for high-stakes public texts.
